metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
Rising colocation rates after a decade of decline are the clearest market signal that AI demand for data center capacity has outrun available supply.

When capacity exceeds demand, prices fall. When supply tightens, prices rise. Rate increases across major metros indicate that colocation providers cannot build or power new facilities fast enough to meet current customer requests. This creates the scarcity condition that matters most for AI scaling: not whether data centers exist, but whether they have available power and space.

For AI workloads specifically, this matters because they consume far more power per unit of compute than previous cloud applications. Higher rates mean customers pay more per kilowatt, which raises the cost structure for every training run and inference deployment. The rate signal also cascades upstream. Rising colocation costs create incentive for hyperscalers to build their own facilities rather than lease, shifting capital flows and construction timelines. It pushes pressure further back onto the grid and the power plants that feed it.

This data tracks price only, not utilization, capacity additions, or geographic variation within metros. It does not explain whether rate rises reflect temporary congestion or structural shortage. It also does not capture the long-term lease contracts that large AI companies negotiate, which may not move as quickly as spot rates. The relationship between colocation rates and grid constraints remains indirect.
